translations.text: The Letter of Mara bar Serapion.
Mara bar Serapion to my son Serapion: greetings. Your teacher and tutor wrote me a letter and told me that you are very diligent in learning, young as you are.
I blessed God because you, a young boy, have begun to think well without a guide. This brought me comfort,
because I heard of your greatness of mind and good conscience, young boy—qualities that do not readily take root in many people.
For this reason I have written you this record of what I have investigated in the world. For I have examined the way people live,
and I pursue learning. All these things I discovered through Greek learning, though they suffer shipwreck at the birth of life.
From now on, my son, apply yourself to what is fitting for free people: reflecting on books and pursuing wisdom.
Resolve, then, to persevere in what you have begun, and diligently remember my instructions, like a thoughtful person who loves discipline.
Even if it seems very bitter to you, when you examine it for a little while, it will become very pleasant to you. For this is how it happened to me too.
A man who has gone away, when he is separated from his family, and can preserve his character and rightly do what he ought—
he is the chosen man who is called a blessing from God, and who finds nothing else to compare with his freedom.
For people who are called to discipline seek to be freed from the struggle of the times.
Those who hold fast to wisdom are sustained by the hope of righteousness. And those who stand firm in truth
show the purpose of their goodness. Those who devote themselves to philosophy seek to escape the world's troubles.
You too, my son, conduct yourself wisely in these matters, like a wise person who seeks to lead a pure life.
Do not let possessions, for which so many people hunger, trouble you, or let your mind turn to desiring wealth, something that does not last.
For possessions do not remain when acquired through [?], nor do they endure when acquired justly. And all these things you see in the world are as though
they will dissolve like a dream after a little while. For they are the rises and falls of the times,
and the empty glory that fills human life. Do you not consider that the very things that delight us soon bring us harm?
This is especially true of the birth of beloved children. For suffering lies in wait for us in either case: the love of good children torments us,
and our attachment to them makes us suffer. With bad children, we struggle to discipline them and are distressed by their misconduct. For I have heard about our companions,
that when they left Samosata, they were grieving and, as it were, blaming the times. They said, “Now we have been taken far from our families,
and we cannot return to our city, see our people, or welcome our gods with praise.” It was fitting that that day
should be called a day of mourning, because the same heavy sorrow gripped them all alike. For as they wept, they remembered their fathers,
and as they lamented, their mothers. They grieved for their brothers and suffered for the women to whom they were betrothed, whom they had left behind.
And when we heard that their former companions were going to Seleucia, we secretly went to meet them on the road and joined our misfortune to theirs.
Then our pain grew much stronger, and with good reason we wept bitterly over our ruin. Our anguish gathered into a dark cloud, and our misery grew greater than a mountain.
For none of us was able to restrain the sorrows within him. Love for the living was stirred up together with grief for the dead.
Our misfortunes were leading us along a pathless way. For we saw our brothers and our children like captives, and we remembered our dead companions, who lay in a land not their own.
Each of us was also worried about himself, lest one misfortune be added to another for him, or another disaster overtake the one before it.
What did the imprisoned men gain by experiencing these things? But you, my dear one, do not be distressed that you have been led from place to place alone.
For human beings are born for this: to endure the reversals of fortune that time brings. Instead, think of it this way: to wise people every place is alike.
And in every city good people have many fathers and mothers. Otherwise, take the evidence from your own experience: how many people who do not know you
love you as their own children, and how many women welcome you as their loved ones! Yet you have prospered as a stranger.
But in return for your little love, many people have responded to you. What, then, can we say about
the error that has settled in the world? Its course through the world is oppressive, and in its upheavals we are shaken like a reed by the wind.
For I was astonished at the many who abandon their children, and I marveled at others who raise children who are not their own. There are people who acquire possessions in the world.
And I also marveled at others who inherit what is not theirs. Understand and see, then, that we walk under the guidance of error.
The sage among men began to say to us: On which of the reeds can a person rely? Or of what things can we speak as though they endure?
On abundant possessions? They are snatched away. On fortresses? They are plundered. On cities? They are ruined. On greatness? It is brought low.
On pride? It is overthrown. On beauty? It fades. On laws? They are transgressed. On poverty? It is despised. On children? They die.
On friends? They prove false. On praise? Envy gets there first. Should someone, then, rejoice in his kingdom like Darius,
or in his good fortune like Polycrates, or in his valor like Achilles, or in his wife like Agamemnon, or in his child like Priam,
or in his skill like Archimedes, or in his wisdom like Socrates, or in his learning like Pythagoras,
or in his brilliance like Palamedes? Human lives, my son, pass away from the world, but their praises and their virtues endure forever.
But you, my young son, choose for yourself something that does not wear out. For those who practice these things
are called modest, beloved, and lovers of a good name. But whenever some misfortune meets you, do not blame anyone.
Do not be angry with God, and do not complain about your times. If you persevere in this way of thinking, your gift will not have been a small one,
the gift received from God, which does not depend on wealth and is not assailed by poverty. For you will live your life without fear,
while you rejoice. For fear and despondency do not lodge with the wise [?], but with those who live outside the law.
For no one has ever been stripped of his wisdom as he has of his possessions. Devote yourself to learning more than to wealth.
For the more possessions increase, the more trouble increases. For I have seen that, for someone whose good things multiply, so too
troubles come to meet him. Where proud displays are carried on, pains also gather, and where possessions increase,
there are many bitter years. If, then, you understand and carefully take heed, neither will God cease helping you nor will people cease loving you.
Let whatever you can acquire be enough for you. But if you can manage without possessions, then you will be called blessed,
and no one will envy you. Remember this too: nothing disturbs your life so very much as possessions.
For no one has been called an owner of possessions after his death. Weak people are taken captive by the desire for possessions, and they do not know that, like a tenant,
a person lives among his possessions. They are anxious because their possessions are not secure. For they have abandoned what is their own and seek what is not their own.
What else, indeed, can we say, when wise people are forcibly led away by the hands of tyrants,
their wisdom is taken captive by slander, and they are stripped of their clarity of mind, with no chance to breathe? For what benefit did the Athenians gain from killing Socrates?
They received famine and plague as their punishment. Or the people of Samos from burning Pythagoras, when in a single hour their whole country was covered in sand?
Or the Jews from their wise king, when from that very time their kingdom was taken away? For God justly exacted retribution for the wisdom of all three.
For the Athenians died of hunger, the people of Samos were engulfed by the sea beyond recovery, and the Jews, devastated and driven from their kingdom,
are scattered everywhere. Socrates did not die, because of Plato; nor did Pythagoras, because of the statue of Hera;
nor did the wise king, because of the new laws he established. But I, my son, have examined people and the evil upheaval in which they live,
and I was astonished that they were not humbled by the evils surrounding them. Not even [?] were enough for them, nor pains, nor illnesses, nor death, nor poverty.
Instead, like savage animals, they attack one another with hostility, competing to see which of them can inflict greater harm on his neighbor. For they have gone beyond the boundary of truth,
and they violate all good laws because they cling to their own desires. For as long as a person longs [?] for what he desires,
how can he do what he rightly ought to do? They recognize no restraint, and they reach out their hands only a little toward truth
and goodness. Instead, they conduct their lives like deaf and blind people. The wicked rejoice, while the righteous are harassed.
The person who has possessions denies it, and the one who has none struggles to acquire them. The poor beg, and the rich hide things away. Everyone laughs at his neighbor.
Some are drunk, others laugh, and others are gripped by anxiety. They rejoice in evil things,
and despise the person [?] who speaks the truth. Should anyone now be surprised when the world wears him down with contempt, when they have no consistent way of life?
They are preoccupied with these things, and one of them looks forward to the time when he will gain the reputation of a victor in battle.
Yet the brave do not consider how many foolish desires take a person captive in the world. If only remorse would touch them even a little!
who prevail by their strength, yet are defeated by greed. For I have tested human beings, and this is how I have tested them:
they look to this one thing alone: an abundance of possessions. Because of this, they do not even have a reliable adviser, but only their changing thoughts.
A person is quickly thrown into sorrow, to be swallowed up by it. They do not consider the world's great wealth, which brings us all alike every kind of trouble [?].
For they have attached themselves to gluttony, the utter disgrace of depraved people. But as for these things that have come into my mind to write to you,
they are not merely for reading; rather, putting them into practice should come first. For I too know that, when you examine this way of life,
it will please you greatly, and you will be free from the evil turmoil we endure for the sake of children and possessions. Therefore rid yourself of sorrow, so cherished by human beings,
a thing that has never been of any use. Banish from yourself anxiety, which brings no benefit. For we have no escape or deliverance
except a great mind capable of bearing misfortunes and enduring the hardships we continually receive at the hands of the times. For these are the things we ought to consider,
not those things that are full of joy and a good reputation. Entrust yourself to wisdom, the fountain of all good things and an inexhaustible treasure.
There you will rest your head and be at peace. For she will be a father and mother to you, and a good companion throughout your life. Let all your attention be devoted to perseverance
and endurance. These can bear the afflictions of weak human beings. For their power is so great that they bear hunger
and endure thirst and relieve every distress. They even make light of toil and suffering. Apply yourself to these things,
and you will lead a tranquil life and be a comfort to me, when you are called the adornment of your ancestors. For in that earlier time,
when our city stood in its greatness, you can know that malicious rumors were spread about many of our people.
We, however, have acknowledged since that time that love is altogether equal [?], and we received honor from its greatness. But time prevented us from completing
the things we had planned in our minds. Even here in prison we give thanks to God that we have received the love of many.
For we are training ourselves to stand firm with wisdom and joy. But if anyone leads us away by force, he will bear witness against himself
that he is far from every good thing. He will receive reproach and shame because of his impure, shameful purpose. For we have demonstrated our truthfulness:
we have committed no offense against the kingdom. But if the Romans allow us to enter our own country, with justice and fairness,
they will act like civilized people and be called good and just, together with the peaceful land in which they live. For they will show their greatness when they leave us as its free citizens.
We will obey the kingdom that the times have given us. Let them not act like tyrants and treat us like slaves.
And if something has been decreed to happen, we will receive nothing more than the peaceful death reserved for us. But you, my young son,
if you wish to understand things diligently, first bring desire under control, and set a limit to whatever you undertake. Endure,
only do not become angry, and instead of [?], listen graciously. For now I am thinking about this: how, so that I may be remembered,
I may leave a book behind me, and with a wise mind complete the journey to which I am condemned, and escape without distress from the world's evil destruction.
For I pray to receive release, and what kind of death it may be does not concern me. But if anyone should be grieved or anxious,
I do not advise him to be so. For there, in the dwelling place of the whole world, these things will await him. One of his friends asked Mara son of Serapion, while he was in chains beside him:
“By your life, Mara, do tell me what amusing thing you have seen that makes you laugh.” Mara said to him:
“I am laughing at time, because although it has borrowed no evil from me, it pays me back.” The letter of Mara son of Serapion is finished.
